result:
The town’s lost-and-found was kept in a shed behind the library. It held the usual things: umbrellas, mittens, a single brass key. But it also held a jar labeled **TUESDAY AFTERNOON**, a paper bag containing the smell of someone’s grandmother’s kitchen, and a small wooden box that rattled whenever anyone nearby almost remembered a name.

The librarian, Mrs. Vale, had stopped asking where the unusual things came from. People brought them in, and she gave them claim tickets, just as she did for the umbrellas.

One morning, a boy arrived carrying nothing at all.

“I think I lost my courage,” he said.

Mrs. Vale took out her ledger. “When did you last have it?”

“Yesterday. I was going to tell my friend I broke his kite.”

“Did you tell him?”

“No.”

She wrote down the boy’s name and gave him a ticket. Then they searched the shed together. They looked under the mittens and behind a row of unclaimed lunchboxes. The wooden box rattled, but it was no help.

At last the boy said, “Maybe it’s at my friend’s house.”

“Quite possible,” said Mrs. Vale. She opened the shed door for him.

He returned that afternoon with a torn kite and his friend beside him. They wanted to know if the library had a book about making kites.

It did. Mrs. Vale helped them find it, and when they left, she crossed the boy’s name out of the ledger.
